opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things people underappreciate. MCTS is only as good as the value function at the leaves. If your value estimates are basically noise, all the search does is spend compute aggregating noise more carefully. You get a lot of expensive rollouts that don't move the policy anywhere useful.

So I think the first step is getting a value function that's at least directionally correct, even if it's not precise. There are a few ways to do that cheaply.

One is supervised bootstrapping. If you have any prior data, like human games, logged trajectories, or demonstrations, you can train the value head to predict outcomes from those states. It'll be biased toward whatever distribution generated the data, but it gives you a ranking signal that's way better than random. AlphaGo did a version of this before AlphaZero showed you could skip it.

Another is to lean on cheap Monte Carlo returns early on. Play out lots of fast, shallow, even random games and regress the value function onto the empirical outcomes. It's high variance, but it's unbiased, and with enough volume the network starts picking up real structure, like material advantage or obviously losing positions. Then you shift toward search-based targets as the value function stabilizes.

I'd also do a curriculum on search budget. Don't start with 800 simulations per move. Start with very few, maybe even close to zero, so you're mostly training on raw policy and outcome data. Then scale up the number of simulations as the value head gets more calibrated. The search earns its compute once the leaf evaluations mean something.

Finally, you need to actually measure calibration. Track how well the predicted value correlates with eventual outcomes on held-out positions, and check whether more search at evaluation time improves play. If doubling the simulations doesn't help, that tells you the value function is the bottleneck, not the search.

The general principle is that search amplifies whatever signal you have. So before you pay for amplification, make sure there's a signal there to amplify.

r001.rationale: The response proposes training on game outcomes and Monte Carlo returns, but does not clearly connect completed-game labels to earlier states while the policy is still uninformative.

r002.rationale: It says MCTS depends on leaf value estimates, recommends making those estimates directionally useful first, and scaling up search only as the value head improves.

r003.rationale: It mentions human games and demonstrations as prior data, but does not clearly specify an offline dataset of realistic, good play or its use for accurate late-game value predictions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people get wrong about AlphaZero is they fixate on the search and forget that the search is only as good as the thing it's bootstrapping off of. MCTS is basically an amplifier. If your value function is noise, you're just amplifying noise, and you burn an enormous amount of compute discovering that.

So my view is you want the cheapest possible signal that's actually correlated with the thing you care about, and you want to get it before you spend a single dollar on deep rollouts. In games that's easy because the environment gives you a terminal reward for free. In the real world, the analogous move is: collect a bunch of trajectories, even bad ones, even random or human ones, and fit a value function on those first. That's offline RL, or you could think of it as just supervised learning on outcomes. The value function doesn't need to be good at the start. It needs to be slightly better than uniform, because that's enough to make the search non-random, and once the search is non-random it starts generating data that's better than what you started with. That's the flywheel.

The other thing I'd say is you should distrust the value function's calibration more than its ranking. For search, what you need is that it orders states correctly, not that it predicts absolute win probability. So I'd evaluate it on pairwise comparisons, like, does it prefer the state that a decent policy would prefer. If it passes that, you can turn on search with a shallow budget, see if the search-improved policy beats the raw policy, and only then scale the tree. If search doesn't beat the raw policy at low depth, more depth is almost never the fix. The value function is the fix.

And honestly the thing I keep coming back to from robotics is that the expensive part is never the algorithm, it's getting the ground truth signal. Whoever has the tightest loop between acting in the world and getting an honest outcome label is going to win, and the elaborate planning on top is kind of a second-order concern.

r001.rationale: It notes that games provide terminal rewards and recommends fitting values from trajectories, but does not explain training predictions for earlier game states from completed-game outcomes while the policy is still uninformative.

r002.rationale: It says to fit a value function before spending on deep rollouts and explains that MCTS amplifies the value function’s signal, so unreliable values make search wasteful.

r003.rationale: It recommends using trajectories, including bad, random, or human ones, but does not state that realistic good play can bootstrap accurate late-game value predictions.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by getting a policy that can produce at least some successful trajectories. That could come from imitation learning, or from reinforcement learning on easier versions of the task. Then you can train a value function on the outcomes: from this state, how likely is the current policy to succeed?

There’s a bootstrapping problem here. If your policy never succeeds, all your value targets are zero, and you haven’t learned much about which states are promising. Search can help you discover successes, but an expensive search guided by a value function that can’t distinguish good states from bad ones isn’t necessarily a great use of compute.

So I’d want to see that the value function can rank candidate continuations reasonably well before scaling up MCTS. Start with a little search, use the improved trajectories to train the policy and value function, and then increase the search budget as those improve. You don’t need a perfect value function upfront; you need enough signal for that feedback loop to get going.

r001.rationale: The response says to train value predictions on successful-trajectory outcomes, but it does not explain using completed-game labels for earlier states while the policy is still uninformative.

r002.rationale: It recommends checking that the value function can rank continuations before scaling up MCTS and explains that search guided by an uninformative value function may waste compute.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention bootstrapping late-game value predictions from an offline dataset of realistic, good play.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by getting a policy that can actually reach successful outcomes some fraction of the time. If you start with a random policy in a very long-horizon problem, almost every rollout fails, and your value function learns that everything is worthless. Running a lot of MCTS on top of that doesn’t necessarily help—you’re spending compute exploring with a signal that can’t distinguish promising states from bad ones.

So you might bootstrap with demonstrations, easier versions of the task, or a curriculum where success is initially within reach. Then you train the value function on actual outcomes from those trajectories. Once it can meaningfully rank the states your policy encounters, search starts to have something useful to work with.

And then you have the feedback loop: search improves the policy, the improved policy generates better experience, and that experience improves the value function. I wouldn’t require a perfect value function before doing any search. I’d just want evidence that a little search improves decisions before spending a huge amount of compute on it.

r001.rationale: It recommends training on actual outcomes from successful trajectories, but does not clearly say that completed games label earlier states while the policy is still uninformative.

r002.rationale: It says to make the value function useful before spending heavily on MCTS because search needs a signal that distinguishes promising states from bad ones.

r003.rationale: It mentions demonstrations and curricula, but not an offline dataset of realistic, good play bootstrapping accurate late-game value predictions.
